parole.significato: Sharpness or acuteness, as of a needle, wit, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English acuite, acuyte, from Middle French acuité, from Medieval Latin acuitas, irreg., from Latin acuō (“sharpen”).

parole.significato: A close physical union of two objects.
parole.testo: From Middle French adhérence, from Latin adhærentia.

parole.significato: The profession of an advocate.
parole.testo: From Middle English advocacie, advocacye, advocatye, from Middle French advocacie, advocatie, avocacie and Medieval Latin advocātia; equivalent to advocate + -cy.

parole.significato: A female advocate.
parole.testo: From Middle French advocatrice, from Old French advocatrice, from Medieval Latin advocatrix.

parole.significato: To be betrothed to; to promise to marry.
parole.testo: From Middle French affiance, from affier (from Medieval Latin affīdāre, from *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere) + -ance.

parole.significato: The process or procedure for allocating things, especially money or other resources.
parole.testo: From Middle French allocacion, from Medieval Latin allocātiō. By surface analysis, allocate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who claims or claimed to be the pope, usually as the result of a disputed election or deposition, but is not c…
parole.testo: From Middle French antipape (later assimilated to anti- + pope), from Medieval Latin antipāpa.

parole.significato: A concise expression of a principle in an area of knowledge; an axiom, a precept.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English amphorisme, from Middle French aphorisme, afforisme (modern French aphorisme), from Medieval Latin aphorismus, aforismus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓φορῐσμός (ăphorĭsmós, “limitation; distinction, separation; definition; aphorism”), from ἀφορίζω (aphorízō, “to

parole.significato: A natural ability to acquire knowledge or skill.
parole.testo: From Middle French aptitude, from Medieval Latin aptitudo, from Latin aptus (“apt, fit”). By surface analysis, apt + -itude. Doublet of attitude.

parole.significato: The condition of being watery; wateriness
parole.testo: From Middle English aquosite, from Middle French, from Medieval Latin aquōsitās, from Latin aquōsus + -itās.

parole.significato: An architect.
parole.testo: From Middle English architectur, from Middle French architecteur, Medieval Latin architector, and Italian architettore, from Latin architectus, architectōn, due to form-association with Latin agent nouns in -tor.

parole.significato: The nobility, or the hereditary ruling class.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French aristocratie, from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best“, that is, “the best-born”, “nobility”), from ἄριστος (áristos, “best, noblest”) + -κρατίᾱ (-kratíā), from κράτος (krátos, “power, rule”). By surface analy

parole.significato: Aid; help; the act or result of assisting.
parole.testo: From Middle English assistance, from Middle French assistance, from Medieval Latin assistentia, from Latin assistō (“to stand at”). By surface analysis, assist + -ance.

parole.significato: A plant (Ocimum basilicum).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English basile, from Middle French basile, from Old French basile, from Medieval Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”). Doublet of basilic, basilicon, and basilicum; further related to basileus, basilean, and basile

parole.significato: The act of beatifying, or the state of being beatified; especially, in the Roman Catholic Church, the act or process of…
parole.testo: From Middle French béatification, from Medieval Latin beātificātiō.

parole.significato: A place where a soldier is assigned to lodge.
parole.testo: From Middle French billette (“schedule”), from bullette, diminutive form of bulle (“document”), from Medieval Latin bulla, hence cognate with etymology 1 above.

parole.significato: A boundary; a limit.
parole.testo: From Middle French borne, from Old French bodne, from Medieval Latin bodina, a word of unknown ultimate origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom, base”), see also Proto-Celtic *bundos.

parole.significato: To supply with a certificate, especially following certification.
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English certificat, certificate, sertyfycat, from Middle French certificat or its etymon Medieval Latin certificātum. The verb is from the noun. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin certificātus.

parole.significato: Synonym of castellan: the lord of a castle; a caretaker entrusted to oversee a castle for its lord.
parole.testo: From Middle English chateleyn, from Middle French chatelaine, from Old French chastelein and castelain (“castellan”), from chastel and castel (“castle”) + -ain (“-an: forming adj.”), from Medieval Latin castellum, from Latin castrum (“fort”) + -ellum (“-elle: forming diminutives”). Doublet of Castil

parole.significato: Surgical.
parole.testo: From Middle English cirurgical, from Middle French cirurgical, from Medieval Latin chirurgicālis.

parole.significato: A dry red wine produced in the Bordeaux region of France, or a similar wine made elsewhere.
parole.testo: From Middle English claret, from Middle French claret, from Medieval Latin clārātum vīnum, from clārus. Compare tent (“Spanish red wine”), also from color. Doublet of clairet.

parole.significato: A temporary group or union of organizations, usually formed for a particular advantage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French coalition, from Medieval Latin coalitiō, coalitiōnem, from Latin coalitus. Compare coalescence.

parole.significato: The settlement of differences by arbitration or by consent reached by mutual concessions.
parole.testo: From Middle French compromis, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin compromissum (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop. neuter of Latin compromissus, past participle of compromittere (“to make a mutual promise to abide by the decision of an arbiter”), from com- (“toge

parole.significato: Having a common center.
parole.testo: From Middle English concentrik, from Middle French concentrique, from Medieval Latin concentricus, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + centrum (“circle, center”). Equivalent to con- + -centric. By surface analysis, con- + centre + -ic.

parole.significato: That which affects one’s welfare or happiness. A matter of interest to someone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French concerner, from Medieval Latin concernō, concernere (“I distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).

parole.significato: The act of consulting together formally; serious conversation or discussion; interchange of views.
parole.testo: From Middle French conférence, from Medieval Latin cōnferentia, from Latin cōnferēns, omitting several steps, from con- + ferō. Compare parallel Russian собра́ние (sobránije), Russian сбо́рище (sbórišče), akin to с- (s-), со- (so-) + брать (bratʹ), ultimately from the same Indo-European prefix and r

parole.significato: To have a common boundary with; to border on.
parole.testo: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.

parole.significato: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.
parole.testo: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).

parole.significato: To conquer.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English conquesten, borrowed from Middle French conquester, from Old French conquester.

parole.significato: Thorough, careful, or vigilant in one’s task performance; painstaking.
parole.testo: From Middle French conscientieux, from Medieval Latin cōnscientiōsus. Its English equivalent could possibly be analyzed as conscient + -ous. See more at conscience.

parole.significato: A melody added to an existing one, especially one added to provide harmony whilst each retains its simultaneous identit…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English [Term?], from Middle French contrepoint, from Medieval Latin contrāpūnctum. Equivalent to counter- + point.

parole.significato: Running; flowing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

parole.significato: Damaging to someone's reputation, especially if untrue.
parole.testo: From Middle French diffamatoire (altered after the prefix de-), from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.

parole.significato: Highly pleasing; delightful, especially to any of the senses; delicious.
parole.testo: From Middle English delectable, from Middle French délectable, from Old French delectable, from Medieval Latin delectare (“to delight”). By surface analysis, delect + -able. Piecewise doublet of delightable.

parole.significato: Rule by the people, especially as a form of government, such as
parole.testo: From Middle French democratie (French démocratie), from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā). By surface analysis, demo- (“people”) + -cracy (“rule”).

parole.significato: A ruler with absolute power; a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

parole.significato: The act of deviating; wandering off the correct or true path or road.
parole.testo: From Middle French deviation, from Medieval Latin deviatio. Morphologically deviate + -ion.

parole.significato: A rolling down.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dévolution, from Medieval Latin devolutio, devolutionis, from Latin devolvo.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or measured across a diameter.
parole.testo: From Middle French dyametral, from Medieval Latin diametrālis.

parole.significato: Something transparent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French diaphane, from Medieval Latin diaphanus (“transparent”), borrowed from Ancient Greek δῐᾰφᾰνής (dĭăphănḗs), from δῐᾰφαίνω (dĭăphaínō, “to shine; to be manifest”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, dia- + -phane.

parole.significato: Synonym of diversify.
parole.testo: Hypercorrection of diversify, on the basis of Latin dīversificō + -ate (verb-forming suffix) with diversify being the regular derived form of Middle French diversifier, itself from Medieval Latin dīversificō, from Latin dīversus (“opposite, different”).

parole.significato: Not at or in the centre; away from the centre.
parole.testo: From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.

parole.significato: Enamel (“an opaque, glossy coating”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French email, from Old French esmal (“enamel”) (modern French émail (“enamel; vitreous enamel; glaze (coating on pottery)”)), from Medieval Latin smaltum (“enamel”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“to melt; to soften”). Doublet of smalt, smalto, and schmaltz.

parole.significato: A leafy salad vegetable, Cichorium endivia, which is often confused with common chicory (Cichorium intybus).
parole.testo: From Middle French endive, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Byzantine Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.

parole.significato: To show or illustrate by example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplifien, from Middle French exemplifier and its etymon Medieval Latin exemplificō, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

parole.significato: Exceeding the bounds of something; roving; hence, foreign.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English extravagaunt, from Middle French extravagant and its etymon Medieval Latin extravagans, present participle of extravagor (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagor (“to wander, stray”).

parole.significato: A fairy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English faie, fei (“a place or person possessed with magical properties”), from Middle French feie, fée (“fairy", "fae”), from Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. More at fairy.

parole.significato: Magical or fairylike.
parole.testo: From Middle English faie, fei (“a place or person possessed with magical properties”), from Middle French feie, fee (“fairy", "fae”), from Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. More at fairy.

parole.significato: Land held of a superior, particularly on condition of homage, fealty, and personal service, especially military service.
parole.testo: From Middle French fief, from Old French fief, from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (whence also Old French fieu, fied), from Old Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle, sheep”), from Proto-Indo-European *peku-, *peḱu- (“sheep”). Doublet of fee, feud, and

parole.significato: A large vessel resembling a jug, usually with a handle, lid, and spout, for serving drinks such as cider or wine at a t…
parole.testo: From Middle English flagon, flakon [and other forms], from Middle French flacon, Old French flacon, flascon (“flask”) (modern French flacon (“vial”)), from Medieval Latin flascōnem, the accusative singular of Late Latin flascō (“bottle; glass or earthenware vessel for wine; portable barrel”), from F

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a brother or brothers.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰréh₂tēr Borrowed from Middle French fraternel, from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or pertaining to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).

parole.significato: A ceremony to honor and remember a deceased person, often distinguished from a memorial service by the presence of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French funerailles pl (“funeral rites”), from Medieval Latin fūnerālia (“funeral rites”), originally neuter plural of Late Latin fūnerālis (“having to do with a funeral”), from Latin fūnus (“funeral, death, corpse”), origin unknown, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *d

parole.significato: To show off.
parole.testo: From Middle English galery, gallerye, from Middle French galerie, gallerie, from Old French galerie, gallerie (“a long portico, a gallery”), from Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of Latin galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea, Galilee, reg

parole.significato: Characterised by a dignified sense of seriousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French grave, a learned borrowing from Latin gravis (“heavy, important”). Compare Old French greve (“terrible, dreadful”). Doublet of grief.

parole.significato: A word or idiom of the Greek language used in another language, especially for literary effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French grecisme (modern French grécisme), from Medieval Latin graecismus, from Classical Latin graecus + -ismus. Compare Middle English Gryscysme (“Graecismus by Eberhard of Béthune”). Doublet of graecismus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to heresy or heretics.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French eretical and from Medieval Latin haereticālis, from haereticus, equivalent to heretic + -al. See heretic.

parole.significato: The position of the planets and stars at the moment of someone's birth; a diagram of such positions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French horoscope, from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”). By surface analysis, horo- + -scope.

parole.significato: A worker employed at an inn, hostelry, or stable to look after horses.
parole.testo: From Middle English hostiler, from Middle French hostiler, from Old French hostelier, from Medieval Latin hostilārius, hospitālārius, from hospitāle "inn", from hospitālis "hospitable", from hospes "host, guest". Both hostler and its alternative form ostler originally meant simply "innkeeper", and a

parole.significato: Relating to the body fluids or humours.
parole.testo: From Middle English humerale, humorale, humoural, from Middle French humoral and Medieval Latin hūmorālis, from Latin hūmor. By surface analysis, humor + -al.

parole.significato: Having a lively or creative imagination.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymagynatif, from Middle French imaginatif, from Medieval Latin imāginātīvus. By surface analysis, imagine + -ative.

parole.significato: Having no matter or substance; incorporeal.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English immaterial, inmateriall (“incorporeal; spiritual”), from Middle French immateriel (“not material”) (modern French immatériel), and from its etymon Medieval Latin immāteriālis (“not material”), from Latin im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’))

parole.significato: To pierce (something) with any long, pointed object.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Medieval Latin impālāre, from Latin palus, whence also pale.

parole.significato: Incapable of being touched or felt; incorporeal, intangible.
parole.testo: From Middle French impalpable, from Medieval Latin impalpabilis. See im- + palpable.

parole.significato: Not perceptible, not detectable, too small in magnitude to be observed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.

parole.significato: The quality or condition of being important or worthy of note.
parole.testo: From Middle English importaunce, from Middle French importance, from Medieval Latin importantia. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ance.

parole.significato: To bother, irritate, trouble.
parole.testo: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".

parole.significato: The act of something happening; occurrence.
parole.testo: From Middle French incidence, from Medieval Latin incidentia (“a falling upon”), from Latin incidens, present participle of incidere (“to fall upon”), from in (“on”) + cadere (“to fall”).

parole.significato: Including (almost) everything within its scope.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French inclusif, from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus + -īvus.

parole.significato: having a ratio that is not expressible as a fraction of two integers.
parole.testo: From Middle French incommensurable, from Medieval Latin incommensurabilis. Its full etymology is equivalent to that of in- + commensurable.

parole.significato: The state of being incongruous, or lacking congruence.
parole.testo: From Middle French incongruité, from Medieval Latin incongruitās, from Latin incongruus.

parole.significato: Absolutely necessary or requisite; that one cannot do without.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French indispensable, from Medieval Latin indispensābilis, corresponding to in- + dispensable.

parole.significato: Capable of burning.
parole.testo: From Middle French inflammable, from Medieval Latin īnflammābilis, from Latin īnflammāre (“to set on fire”), from in (“in, on”) + flamma (“flame”). By surface analysis, inflame + -able, literally “able to be inflamed”.

parole.significato: Unbreakable, indestructible, or very difficult to break.
parole.testo: From Middle French infrangible, from Old French infrangible, from Medieval Latin in- (“not”) + frangibilis, from Latin frangō (“to break”).

parole.significato: Not inclined to hospitality; unfriendly.
parole.testo: From Middle French inhospitable, from Medieval Latin inhospitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + hospitable.

parole.significato: An act of installing.
parole.testo: From Middle French installation, from Medieval Latin installātiō. By surface analysis, install + -ation. Compare with Piedmontese istallassion.

parole.significato: Instinct, incitement, or inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle English instinccion, instyncyon, from Middle French instincion and its etymon Medieval Latin īnstīnctiō.

parole.significato: Incapable of being perceived by the senses; incorporeal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.

parole.significato: Constituting a whole together with other parts or factors; not omittable or removable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French integral, from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer (“entire”); see integer.

parole.significato: Immediate cognition without the use of conscious rational processes.
parole.testo: From Middle French intuition, from Medieval Latin intuitiō (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueor (“to look at, consider”), from in- (“in, on”) + tueor (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”). Equivalent to intuit + -ion.

parole.significato: Spontaneous, without requiring conscious thought.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French intuitif, from Medieval Latin intuitivus, from Latin intueri.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to invasion; offensive.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁én The adjective is derived from Middle English invasif (“of a weapon: offensive”), from Middle French invasif, Old French invasif (“invasive”) (modern French invasif), from Medieval Latin invāsīvus, from Latin invāsus (“entered; invaded”) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives). Invāsus is

parole.significato: An expression which inveighs or rails against a person.
parole.testo: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). See vehicle, and compare with inveigh.

parole.significato: The act of investing, as with possession or power; formal bestowal or presentation of a possessory or prescriptive righ…
parole.testo: From Middle French investiture, from Medieval Latin investītūra, from investīre (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: An instance of being irregular.
parole.testo: From Middle French irrégularité, from Medieval Latin irregularitas. Morphologically irregular + -ity.

parole.significato: One skilled in the law.
parole.testo: From Middle French légiste, from Medieval Latin lēgista, from Latin lex (“law”). Compare legal.

parole.significato: The process of making or declaring a person legitimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English legittimacion, from Middle French legitimacion and its etymon, Medieval Latin lēgitimātiō, lēgitimātiōnem, from lēgitimāre (“to legitimate”), from Latin lēgitimus. By surface analysis, legitimate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of being, or state of having been, made liquid (from either a solid or a gas).
parole.testo: From Middle English liquefaction, from Middle French liquefaction (modern French liquéfaction), from Medieval Latin liquefactiō.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being livid.
parole.testo: From Middle English lividite, lyvydite, from Middle French lividité and its etymon Medieval Latin līviditās, from Latin līvidus (“livid”) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, livid + -ity.

parole.significato: A complex structure, such as a society, considered as a single entity that contains numerous similar, smaller-scale str…
parole.testo: From Middle French macrocosme (from Old French macrocosme) and Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”).

parole.significato: More than half (50%) of some group.
parole.testo: From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.

parole.significato: The planned movement of troops, vehicles etc.; a strategic repositioning; (later also) a large training field-exercise…
parole.testo: From Middle French manœuvre (“manipulation, maneuver”) and manouvrer (“to maneuver”), from Old French manovre (“handwork, manual labor”), from Medieval Latin manopera, manuopera (“work done by hand, handwork”), from manu (“by hand”) + operari (“to work”). First recorded in the Capitularies of Charle

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of maneuver.
parole.testo: From Middle French manœuvre (“manipulation, manoeuvre”) and manouvrer (“to manoeuvre”), from Old French manovre (“handwork, manual labour”), from Medieval Latin manopera, manuopera (“work done by hand, handwork”), from manu (“by hand”) + operari (“to work”). First recorded in the Capitularies of Cha

parole.significato: The action or process of making goods systematically or on a large scale.
parole.testo: From Middle French manufacture, from Old French, from Medieval Latin manūfactūra (“a making by hand”), from manūfactus, a compound of manū factus, manū being ablative of manus (“hand”), and factus past participle of faciō (“to do, make”). Compare manual, facture.

parole.significato: A bird, the martin.
parole.testo: From Middle English martilet, probably a blend of martinet (“martin”; from Middle French martinet and Medieval Latin martineta) and Middle French merlet.

parole.significato: The killing of a considerable number (usually limited to people) where little or no resistance can be made, with indisc…
parole.testo: 1580, from Middle French massacre, from Old French macacre, marcacre, macecre, macecle (“slaughterhouse, butchery”), usually thought to be deverbal from Old French macecrer, macecler (“to slaughter”), though the noun seems to be attested somewhat earlier. It is also found in Medieval Latin mazacrium

parole.significato: A remedy used in medieval medicine to promote maturation; a maturant.
parole.testo: From Middle English maturatif, from Middle French maturatif, from Medieval Latin mātūrātīvus. By surface analysis, mature + -ative or maturate + -ive.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a mode or modus.
parole.testo: From Middle French modal, from Medieval Latin modālis (“pertaining to a mode”), from Latin modus (“mode”). Compare to French, Spanish, and Portuguese modal and Italian modale. By surface analysis, mod(e) + -al.

parole.significato: Any shoe with an upper covering the front of the foot but without a back flap or strap, leaving the heel exposed.
parole.testo: From Middle French mule (“backless slipper”), from Medieval Latin mula (“slipper, shoe with a thick sole”), presumably from classical Latin mulleus, the dyed shoe of either the patricians or senators, from mūllus (“red mullet”) + -eus (“-y: forming adjectives”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).

parole.significato: A shellfish which contains mother-of-pearl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nacre, from Medieval Latin nacchara, ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra). Doublet of nagara, nagada, naqareh, and naker. Also present in nacarat.

parole.significato: Any substance or drug that reduces pain, induces sleep and may alter mood or behaviour; in some contexts, especially in…
parole.testo: From Middle English narcotyk, from Middle French narcotique (from Old French narcotique, noun use of adjective) and directly from Medieval Latin narcōticum, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτῐκόν (narkōtĭkón), neuter of ναρκωτῐκός (narkōtĭkós), from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “to benumb”), from νάρκη (nár

parole.significato: A kind of small turnip, a variety of Brassica napus.
parole.testo: From Middle French naveau, navel, from Old French naveau, navel, from Medieval Latin nāpellus, a diminutive of Latin nāpus (“turnip, rapeseed, etc”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being neutral; the condition of being unengaged in contests between others; state of taking no…
parole.testo: From Middle French neutralité, from Medieval Latin neutralitas. Morphologically neutral + -ity.

parole.significato: The state of being null, or void, or invalid.
parole.testo: From Middle French nullité and its etymon Medieval Latin nūllitās, from Latin nūllus. By surface analysis, null + -ity.

parole.significato: The nape of the neck.
parole.testo: From Middle French nuque, nuche, from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ). Doublet of nucha.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a material object, actual existence or reality.
parole.testo: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. By surface analysis, object + -ive.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or located within or near the occiput (back of the head) or the occipital bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle French occipital, from Medieval Latin occipitālis, from occiput (“the back of the head, occiput”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent of occiput + -al. Doublet of occipitalis.

parole.significato: An actual instance when a situation occurs; an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Middle French occurrence, from Medieval Latin occurrentia. Morphologically occur + -ence.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the eye or to vision.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French optique or Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτῐκός (optĭkós, “of or for sight”), from ὀπτός (optós, “visible”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A musician who plays the organ.
parole.testo: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

parole.significato: The quality of being organized.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French organisation, from Medieval Latin organizātiō; by surface analysis, organize + -ation.

parole.significato: To arrange in working order.
parole.testo: From Middle English organizen, organysen, partly from Middle French organiser and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin organizō, from Latin organum (“organ”). By surface analysis, organ + -ize.

parole.significato: Of two objects, at right angles; perpendicular to each other.
parole.testo: From Middle French orthogonal, in turn from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis and Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρθογώνιος (orthogṓnios, “rectangular”). By surface analysis, ortho- + -gon + -al.

parole.significato: A native, citizen and/or inhabitant of Paris, France
parole.testo: From Middle English Parisien, perisien, from Middle French parisien, from Medieval Latin parisiānus. By surface analysis, Paris + -ian.

parole.significato: Preference, bias in favor of, tendency.
parole.testo: From Middle English parcialite, parcialtee, parcyalte, partialte, percialite, from Middle French partialité and its etymon Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partialitas.

parole.significato: A patriarchal system or community.
parole.testo: From Middle French patriarcat, from Old French patriarcat, from Medieval Latin patriarchatus, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “patriarch”). By surface analysis, patriarch + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it, a body of people involved with it).

parole.significato: A length of time.
parole.testo: From Middle English periode, from Middle French periode, from Medieval Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, orbit, a recurring interval of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”). Displaced native Middle English tide (“interval, period, sea

parole.significato: The state of being permanent.
parole.testo: From Middle English permanence, permanens, from Middle French permanence, from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

parole.significato: Of a person: having a pleasing appearance; attractive; handsome.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English personable, personabil (“having a pleasing appearance, handsome”), and then from both of the following: * For sense 1 (“having a pleasing appearance”) and sense 2 (“having a pleasant manner”) (these senses are not found in Old French or Medieval Latin), probably from person,

parole.significato: Able to persuade; convincing.
parole.testo: From Middle French persuasif, from Medieval Latin persuāsīvus, from Latin past participle stem of persuādēre + -īvus.

parole.significato: To turn to stone: to harden organic matter by permeating with water and depositing dissolved minerals.
parole.testo: From Middle French pétrifier, from Medieval Latin petrificāre, from Latin petra (“rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + -ficāre, from facere (“do, make”), equivalent to petro- + -ify.

parole.significato: A place where prescription drugs are sold or dispensed.
parole.testo: From Middle English pharmacy, borrowed from Middle French pharmacie (“the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative”), from Old French farmacie, from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantm

parole.significato: Power or strength; potency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French potence (“power, a crutch”), from Latin potentia (“power, in Medieval Latin also crutch”), from potens (“powerful”); see potent.

parole.significato: Repetition of an activity to improve a skill.
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English practice, practique, practyse, from the verb; also compare Medieval Latin prāctica.. Displaced native Old English sidu. The verb is from Middle English practice, practise, practize, practyse, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, alteration of practiquer, from Medie

parole.significato: To repeat (an activity) as a way of improving one's skill in that activity.
parole.testo: From Middle English practizen, a variant of practisen, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, from Medieval Latin practizo, from Late Latin practico (“to do, perform, execute, propose, practise, exercise, be conversant with, contrive, conspire, etc.”), from prāctica (“practical affairs", "business”

parole.significato: Permission to use a port given to a ship after compliance with quarantine or on conviction that she is free of contagio…
parole.testo: Originated 1600–10. Borrowed from Middle French practique, pratique, from Medieval Latin prāctica. Doublet of practice.

parole.significato: A stipend paid to a canon of a cathedral.
parole.testo: From Middle French prebende, from Medieval Latin prebenda, from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Doublet of provender.

parole.significato: Common or widespread; prevalent.
parole.testo: From Middle French prédominant, ultimately from Medieval Latin praedominans. By surface analysis, pre- + dominant.

parole.significato: The selection of one thing or person over others (with the main adposition being "for" in relation to the thing or pers…
parole.testo: From Middle French preference, from Medieval Latin preferentia. Doublet of preferans. Morphologically prefer + -ence. Compare typologically Russian предвзя́тость (predvzjátostʹ) (<< взять (vzjatʹ), a suppletive of брать (bratʹ), which is cognate with Latin ferō).

parole.significato: An introductory or preliminary performance or event.
parole.testo: From Middle French prélude (“singing to test a musical instrument”), from Medieval Latin preludium, from Latin praelūdere.

parole.significato: That serves to prepare something
parole.testo: From Middle English preperatif, from Middle French preparatif and Medieval Latin prēparātīvus.

parole.significato: The person who proposes a contract (or one of its clauses)
parole.testo: From Middle French proference, from Medieval Latin proferentia. Doublet of proferans.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the characteristics of prose.
parole.testo: From Middle French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prosa (“prose”), from prorsus (“straightforward, in prose”), from Old Latin provorsus (“straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn,

parole.significato: The prostate gland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French prostate, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prostata.

parole.significato: Any of the first Christian martyrs.
parole.testo: From Middle English prothomartir, prothomartyr, from Middle French prothomartir and Medieval Latin prōtomartyr, from Koine Greek πρωτομάρτυς (prōtomártus). By surface analysis, proto- + martyr.

parole.significato: Inflicting punishment; punishing.
parole.testo: From Middle French punitif, from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).

parole.significato: The act or process of qualifying for a position, achievement etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French qualification in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin quālificātiō. By surface analysis, qual(ify) + -ification.

parole.significato: Any of the three points that divide an ordered distribution into four parts, each containing a quarter of the populatio…
parole.testo: From Middle French quartil, from Medieval Latin quartilus. By surface analysis, quart + -ile.

parole.significato: A thing that is the most perfect example of its type; the most perfect embodiment of something; epitome, prototype.
parole.testo: PIE word  *pénkʷe From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia (“fifth essence, aether”), equivalent to quint- + essence. "Essence" in this context is a synonym for "element". In pre-atomic/Aristotelian theory, there are four known elements or essences — Eart

parole.significato: A branching-out, the act or result of developing branches; specifically the divergence of the stem and limbs of a plant…
parole.testo: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.

parole.significato: To divide into branches or subdivisions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ramifier, from Medieval Latin ramificō (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + -ficō (causative suffix).

parole.significato: The act or process of ratifying, or the state of being ratified.
parole.testo: From Middle French ratification, from Medieval Latin ratificatio.

parole.significato: Repeat undertaking or restoration.
parole.testo: From reconduct + -ion. Borrowed from Middle French reconduction in the “repeat lease” sense, itself from Medieval Latin recondūctiō from recondūcere already used by classical Roman jurisprudence.

parole.significato: Any quadrilateral having opposing sides parallel and four right angles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum (“right angle”), from Latin rectus (“right”) + angulus (“an angle”).

parole.significato: Any of certain residences for clergy members.
parole.testo: From Middle French rectorie, from Medieval Latin rectoria. See rector.

parole.significato: A relationship or relation (to something).
parole.testo: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns, present participle of referō (“return, reply”, literally “carry back”). Morphologically refer + -ence.

parole.significato: The process of rehabilitating somebody or something.
parole.testo: From Middle French réhabilitation, from Medieval Latin rehabilitatio.

parole.significato: Typical; having the same properties or interest as a larger group.
parole.testo: From Middle English representative, from Middle French representatif and its etymon Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus. By surface analysis, represent + -ative; See representation. Displaced native Old English spala (“a representative”).

parole.significato: Tending to rouse aversion or to repulse; disgusting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French repulsif, from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus. By surface analysis, repuls(e) + -ive. Compare typologically Polish odpychający (< pchnąć), Russian отта́лкивающий (ottálkivajuščij) (< толкну́ть (tolknútʹ)).

parole.significato: Having power to retain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French rétentif, from Old French retentif, from Medieval Latin retentivus, from Latin retentus.

parole.significato: Capable of being saved.
parole.testo: From Middle English savable, from Middle French sauvable, from Old French salvable, sauvable, from Medieval Latin salvābilis; equivalent to save + -able.

parole.significato: Related or connected to science
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French scientifique, from Medieval Latin scientificus (“pertaining to science”).

parole.significato: Having the faculty of sensation; pertaining to the senses.
parole.testo: From Middle French sensitif, from Medieval Latin sensitivus. By surface analysis, sense + -ite + -ive.

parole.significato: The combination of circumstances at a given moment; a state of affairs.
parole.testo: From Middle English situacioun, situacion, from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”). By surface analysis, situate + -ion.

parole.significato: An explicit set of requirements to be satisfied by a material, product, or service.
parole.testo: From Middle French specification, from Medieval Latin specificationem (accusative of specificatio).

parole.significato: A buttery or pantry.
parole.testo: From Middle English spence, spense, borrowed from Middle French despense, from Medieval Latin dīspēnsa, noun use of feminine of Latin dīspēnsus, past participle of dīspendere (“weigh out”).

parole.significato: A curve that is the locus of a point that rotates about a fixed point while continuously increasing its distance from t…
parole.testo: From Middle French spirale, from Medieval Latin spiralis, from Latin spīra, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “wreath, coil, twist”).

parole.significato: To transform from an earthly body into a celestial body; to place in the sky as such
parole.testo: From Middle English stellifien (“to make into a star; glorify, deify”), from Middle French stellifier, from Medieval Latin stellificāre, itself from Latin stella (“star”) + faciō (“make, do”).

parole.significato: Used for sublimation.
parole.testo: From Middle French sublimatoire, from Medieval Latin sublīmātōrius.

parole.significato: The process of making or classing (something or somebody) as subordinate.
parole.testo: From Middle French subordination, from Medieval Latin subordinatio.

parole.significato: An indirect or deceptive device or stratagem; a blind. Refers especially to war and diplomatics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge m, from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, used in, or resulting from surgery.
parole.testo: From Middle English cirurgical, borrowed from Middle French cirurgical, from Medieval Latin cirurgicālis, ultimately from Ancient Greek χειρουργία (kheirourgía), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). Replaced Old English Old English læċe (“doctor, physician”). By surface analysis, surge

parole.significato: A perennial herb, the wormwood species Artemisia dracunculus, from Europe and parts of Asia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French targon (cf. modern estragon), from Medieval Latin tragonia, from Arabic طَرْخُون (ṭarḵūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion, “dragonwort, Dracunculus vulgaris”), from δράκων (drákōn, “dragon, serpent”). Doublet of estragon.

parole.significato: Money or goods collected by a government (or an entity to whom the government has delegated this power, e.g. in tax far…
parole.testo: From Middle English taxe, from Middle French taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa, from Latin taxō (“to appraise, value, estimate; (medieval) to tax”). Doublet of task. Displaced native Old English gafol, which was also the word for “tribute” and “rent”.

parole.significato: To deliberately act evasively or prolong a discussion in order to gain time or postpone a decision, sometimes so that a…
parole.testo: From Middle French temporiser (“to wait one's time, temporize”) + English -ize (suffix forming verbs). Temporiser is derived from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin temporāre (“to delay, put off”) + -izāre (suffix forming the present active infinitive of verbs). Temporāre is derived from tempor-

parole.significato: A dog from a group of small, lively breeds, originally bred for the hunting of burrowing prey such as rats, rabbits, fo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French chien terrier (“terrier dog”), from chien (“dog”) + Old French terrier (“of earth”, adjective), from Medieval Latin terrarius (“of earth”), from Latin terra (“earth”).

parole.significato: A form of government in which ambition for honor, power and military glory motivates the rulers.
parole.testo: 1580s, from Middle French tymocracie, from Medieval Latin (13th century) timocratia, from Ancient Greek τῑμοκρατίᾱ (tīmokratíā), from τῑμή (tīmḗ, “valuation; honor”) + -κρατίᾱ (-kratíā, “a rule, reign”), from κρατέω (kratéō, “to rule”) (see -cracy).

parole.significato: The loss of water by evaporation in terrestrial plants, especially through the stomata; accompanied by a corresponding…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transpiration, from Medieval Latin transpiratio, from transpiro, from Latin trans + spiro.

parole.significato: To give off (vapour, waste matter etc.); to exhale (an odour etc.).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transpirer, from Medieval Latin transpirare (“to breathe through”), from Latin trans (“across”) spirare (“to breathe”). The sense “to become known” is also present in French, while the sense “to happen” is not; the latter probably developed in English from the former.

parole.significato: The act or process of transposing or interchanging.
parole.testo: From Middle French transposition, from Medieval Latin transpositio.

parole.significato: Running or lying across; transverse.
parole.testo: From Middle French transversal, from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus.

parole.significato: Identical pitch between two notes or sounds; the simultaneous playing of notes of identical pitch (or separated by one…
parole.testo: From Middle English unisoun, from Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus (“having the same sound”), from ūni- + sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: A vacation.
parole.testo: From Middle French vacance, from Medieval Latin vacantia. Doublet of vacancy.

parole.significato: A man's personal male attendant, responsible for his clothes and appearance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French valet, from Old French vaslet, from Medieval Latin *vassellittus, diminutive of Late Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and

parole.significato: Plants, taken collectively.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French végétation, from Medieval Latin vegetātiōnem.

parole.significato: Of or relating to plants; especially to their growth.
parole.testo: From Middle French végétatif, from Medieval Latin vegetativus, from past participle stem of vegetare.

parole.significato: Quality of being venomous or poisonous.
parole.testo: From Middle English venenosite, venenositee, venenoste, venenouste, from Middle French venenosite or Medieval Latin venēnōsitas. By surface analysis, venene + -osity. Piecewise doublet of venomosity.

parole.significato: The quality of speaking or stating the truth; truthfulness.
parole.testo: From Middle French véracité, from Old French veracitie, from Medieval Latin vērācitās (“truthfulness”) (whence -acity), from Latin vērāx (“truthful, speaking truth”), from vērus (“true, real”). See very.

parole.significato: The act or process of verifying.
parole.testo: From Middle French verification (modern French vérification) or its etymon Medieval Latin vērificātiō. By surface analysis, verificate + -ion.

parole.significato: A specific form or variation of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiō, from Latin vertō (“to turn”). Used in English since 16th century.

parole.significato: Vindicating, having a tendency to vindicate.
parole.testo: From Middle French vindicatif, from Medieval Latin vindicativus.

parole.significato: The state of being viscous.
parole.testo: From Middle French viscosité, from Old French viscosité, from Medieval Latin viscositas; analysable as viscous + -ity.

parole.significato: A pick and hatchet in one tool for tearing down hedges.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English besagu, besague, from Middle French besague, from Old French besague, besagude, from Medieval Latin bisacūta. Doublet of besague.
